Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> International | National | Top Story Murdered Ghanaian teenager Javits laid to rest in New York as Mamdani, Al Sharpton, others pay tribute Source : Kenneth Awotwe Darko 20 November 2026 6:28pm ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
Family, friends, community leaders and public officials gathered in the Bronx, New York, on Friday, November 20, to bid farewell to 15-year-old Ghanaian teenager Badu Nkansah Frimpong, popularly known as Javits, who was fatally shot last month.
The funeral brought together New York City Mayor-elect Zohran Kwame Mamdani, civil rights activist Rev. Al Sharpton, Ghanaian officials and other dignitaries to pay tribute to the teenager whose death has left his family and community devastated.
In his address, Mamdani said New York would forever be proud to call Javits one of its own, despite the short time he spent in the city.
He described him as an extraordinary son, brother and friend who had an uncommon sense of purpose and was determined to make a difference in the lives of others.
Mamdani said Javits had hoped to pursue an education, join the military and become a doctor, describing his ambitions as a reflection of his commitment to service.
'Mema mo yaakor' - New York City Major, Zohran Kwame Mamdani, in Akan language, pays tribute to 15-year-old Javits at funeral in the US. Full tribute of @NYCMayor. https://t.co/lu913DMo88
The Mayor-elect, who also moved to New York from Africa as a child, said the teenager represented the hopes of many young immigrants who travel to the United States in search of better opportunities.
He expressed sadness that Javits' life had been cut short before he could realise his ambitions, urging mourners to honour his memory by showing love and serving others.
Mamdani also acknowledged the Ghanaian community, both at home and in the diaspora, for its contribution to helping Africans recognise their worth and purpose.
He expressed pride in his middle name, Kwame, which he said his father gave him in honour of Ghana's first President, Dr Kwame Nkrumah.
Rev. Al Sharpton, who delivered the eulogy, called for unity between African Americans and African immigrants, urging both communities to confront hostility and divisions among people of African descent.
He said growing prejudice against immigrants, including hostility towards people because of their accents and places of birth, was affecting children.
‘You couldn’t become a doctor, but we’ll use you to heal the community’ – American civil rights activist, Al Sharpton to the late Javits at his funeral in the Bronx. https://t.co/sD8zMmYb05
Sharpton urged parents to use Thanksgiving family gatherings to teach their children not to hate others and to embrace people from different backgrounds.
“We are all African, some displaced African, some at home African, we're all African,” he said.
He acknowledged that the full circumstances surrounding Javits' killing were not established but insisted that the consequences of the violence required a collective response.
Sharpton also drew on the biblical story of Joseph and his brothers to warn against jealousy and hostility, calling on the community to confront what he described as self-hatred, anti-immigrant sentiment and divisions among Black people.
In his closing remarks, he said Javits could still inspire healing within the community despite never getting the opportunity to fulfil his ambition of becoming a doctor.
“Javits, even though you never went to medical school, you became a doctor. We're going to use you to heal the community,” he said.
The funeral programme also featured tributes from Javits' parents and siblings, who remembered him as an ambitious young boy with dreams of becoming a doctor and giving back to people in need.
His father recalled receiving a police call informing him that his son had been shot. He said he had worked hard to bring Javits from Ghana to the United States in the hope of giving him better opportunities.
“I was supposed to celebrate your achievements, not stand beside your grave,” he said in his tribute.
Javits' mother, who described him as her only son, said he had hoped to become a doctor, return to Ghana and care for her as well as help the less privileged.
“If a mother's tears could bring back a child, I would have cried you back into my arms,” she said.
Javits was born on April 29, 2011, and moved from Ghana to the United States in 2025 to join his father and pursue his education. He was fatally shot in the Bronx on October 29, 2026, aged 15.
